metadata.title: Understanding teacher leadership: Development and testing of the survey of teacher leadership

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected survey responses from Nevada public-school teachers (non-charter) via email invitations and Qualtrics in fall 2022, with 1,274 respondents completing all or part of the survey. The methodology describes defining the target population as all non-charter public-school teachers in Nevada and does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is focused on instrument development and psychometric validation (CFA/IRT) rather than population-representative estimation, the manuscript does not specify any weighting variable to adjust estimates to a broader teacher population. Missingness was handled via listwise deletion for CFA/SEM-style estimation, and the two-phase scale refinement/validation used an even/odd split of observations rather than a weighted survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are survey responses measuring teacher self-efficacy and behavioral frequency on Likert-type items, and the study’s core analyses are CFA and IRT graded response models for instrument validation rather than PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. The paper therefore does not generate or analyze PVs as in ILSA achievement domains.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Target population was defined as all Nevada public-school teachers who were not teaching in charter schools. Teacher emails were retrieved from districts and school websites; 20,168 email addresses were collected and invitations were sent via Qualtrics in fall 2022, with two follow-up reminders. The analytic sample comprised 1,274 teachers who completed all or a portion of the survey (response rate 6.32%). For psychometric analyses, item-level missingness ranged from 2 to 6% across items and listwise deletion was used; data were then split into two subsamples using even-numbered observations for phase 1 and odd-numbered observations for phase 2.

main_findings.dataset_used: ILSA literature synthesis (systematic review; no single student-level analytic micro-dataset)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ILSA literature synthesis (systematic review; no single student-level analytic micro-dataset) the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper develops and validates a new instrument—the Survey of Teacher Leadership (STL)—for measuring five teacher leadership subtypes: professional growth, professional development leadership, collaboration, shared leadership, and equity leadership. Data were collected from 1,274 non-charter public-school teachers in Nevada (USA) via an email/Qualtrics survey in fall 2022, with item responses captured as both self-efficacy (4-point Likert) and behavioral frequency (6-point Likert). The authors used a two-phase approach: CFA with WLSMV estimation for construct validity and scale refinement, followed by graded response IRT models to examine item and scale functioning; model fit was evaluated using CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR and item-level fit indices. Missing item responses were handled with listwise deletion, and the final measurement models were validated on an independent even/odd split. Reliability was supported with Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega exceeding 0.77 across subscales, and the final CFA/IRT models showed adequate-to-excellent fit (e.g., RMSEA≤0.07, CFI≥0.97, TLI≥0.98). Because the study is instrument validation rather than predictive modeling, it does not estimate ML performance metrics or causal effects. This indicates that RT models showed adequate-to-excellent fit (e.g., RMSEA≤0.07, CFI≥0.97, TLI≥0.98). Because the study is instrument validation rather than predictive modeling, it does not estimate ML performance metrics or causal effects.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical large-scale assessment prediction study using ILSA microdata; it is a survey instrument development and psychometric validation paper. As a result, there are no ILSA program/cycle/grade/domain achievement outcomes, no Plausible Values, no ML algorithms, and no predictive target variables with performance metrics to populate main_findings.
